**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verses 6–9:**

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is All-Wise, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿When Moses said to his family, "Indeed, I have perceived a fire. I will bring you from it some news, or bring you a burning brand that you may warm yourselves."﴾ ﴿But when he came to it, he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it. And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿"O Moses, indeed it is I, Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Wise."﴾

"Talqā" is a form of "tafaʿala," doubled (mudaʿʿaf), and its meaning is "tuʿṭā" (you are given). As He, glorified is He, said: ﴿But none receives it except those of great fortune﴾ [Fussilat: 35]. Al-Hasan said: the meaning is that you receive the Qur'an.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no doubt that the grace of Allah the Exalted overflows upon him, and He causes him (ﷺ) to receive it. This verse is a refutation of the Quraysh disbelievers in their claim that the Qur'an came from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah of his own accord. "Min ladun" means: from Him and from His direction. "Al-Ḥakīm" means: one possessing wisdom in knowing where to place His messages, and in other matters. There is no god but He.

Then He, the Exalted, related the account of Moses; the implied meaning is: "Mention when Moses said..." Part of Moses' situation, peace be upon him, was that when he set out with his wife, the daughter of Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both, intending Egypt, and the time of his prophethood had drawn near, they walked on a dark, cold, rainy night. They lost the fire, the cold afflicted them, the darkness intensified upon them, and they lost the way. Moses' firestriker (zinād) failed to produce a spark. While he was in this state, he saw a fire at a distance. "Ānastu" means: I saw, and from it comes the saying of Ḥassān ibn Thābit:

"Look, my friend, at the gate of Jillaq: do you perceive anyone beyond al-Balqa'?"

When Moses saw that, he said to his family what is in the verse, and he walked toward it. When he drew near to it, it receded from him. That was a light from the light of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and it was not fire in itself, but Moses supposed it to be fire. Then Allah, blessed and exalted, called to him at that moment, and Moses, peace be upon him, heard the call from the direction of the tree, and Allah the Exalted made him hear His speech. "Al-khabar" which Moses, peace be upon him, hoped for is the information about the way. As for His saying ﴿with a burning brand (shihāb qabas)﴾, He likened the fire found at the tip of a stick or other object to a shihāb (a brand), then specified it as being something taken from a fire (iqtibās), since shuhub (meteors/brands) may occur without being taken from a fire. "Qabas" is a noun for a piece of fire taken from a stick or other object, just as "qabḍ" is a noun for what is grasped. From it comes the verse of Abu Zayd:

"In his grip is a spear-shaft, well-straightened, in which is a point like the flame of a qabas."

(p-518) And the saying of another:

"Whoever wishes, let him take a brand from the fire of the Hellfire."

The origin of shihāb is a star that falls in pursuit of an eavesdropping devil, and everything among the luminous bodies called shihāb is by way of comparison. Al-Zajjaj said: every white thing that has light is a shihāb, but his statement is open to objection. "Qabas" may be a noun, not an adjective, which is then construed as a genitive: meaning "a shihāb which he took" or "which it took." If it is an adjective, this is like the idafa of "al-dār" to "al-ākhira," and "al-ṣalāh" to "al-ūlā," and other such constructions. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "shihāb" as genitive-linked to "qabas," which is the reading of al-Hasan and the people of Madina, Makka and Syria. 'Āṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī read "bi-shihābin qabasin" with tanwīn on "shihāb," and this is in the sense of an adjective; it may also be a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "qabasa yaqbisu," just as "al-ḥalb" is the maṣdar of "ḥalaba yaḥlibu." Abu al-Hasan said: the idafa is better and more common in recitation, as you say "dār ājurr" and "siwār dhahab," as reported by Abu 'Ali. "Taṣṭalūn" means: you warm yourselves against the cold.

The pronoun in "jā'ahā" refers to the fire which Moses, peace be upon him, saw. As for His, blessed and exalted, saying ﴿an-bōrika﴾, the "an" may be explanatory (mufassira), it may be in the accusative position with the implied meaning "bi-an bōrika," or it may be in the nominative position with the implied meaning "nūdiya annahu," as said by al-Zajjaj. As for "bōrika," its meaning is: sanctified, its good multiplied and increased. Barakah is specific to good, and from this is the saying of Abu Talib ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib:

"Blessed is the strange dead man, as the pomegranate-stalk and the olive are blessed."

"Bāraka" is transitive without a preposition; the Arabs say: "Bārakaka Allāh" (may Allah bless you).

(p-519) As for His, exalted is He, saying ﴿whoever is in the fire﴾, the interpreters differed concerning it. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and others said: He, Mighty and Majestic, meant Himself, and some of them expressed this view in disapproved and objectionable terms. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He meant the Light. Al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas said: by "whoever is around it" He meant the angels and Moses.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for the statement of al-Hasan and others, it can only be construed by omitting a modifier (muḍāf), meaning: "blessed is (what comes) from His power and authority in the fire," and the meaning is: "in the fire" according to your supposition and what you reckoned. As for the view that "whoever is in the fire" is the Light, this is on the basis that the Light is referred to in terms of its being the light of Allah the Exalted; and it may be that it refers to the angels, because that light which Moses supposed to be fire was not free of angels. "Whoever is around it" would be Moses and the angels surrounding it. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "bōrikati al-nāru" (the fire was blessed). And "min ḥawlihā" would be Moses and the angels; so Abu Ḥatim reported. Ibn Makki reported that he recited "tabārakati al-nāru wa-man ḥawlahā," and Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported that he recited "wa-man ḥawlahā min al-malā'ikah" (and whoever is around it of the angels). He said: Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima and Mujahid likewise recited thus.

As for His, exalted is He, saying ﴿And exalted is Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, it may be that it is among what was said in the call to Moses, peace be upon him, (p-520) and it may be that it is an address to Muhammad (ﷺ) as an interjection between the two statements. The purpose of it, on both views, is the glorification of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, from whatever might occur to the mind regarding the meaning of the call from the tree and the idea that His power and authority are in the fire. The return of "man" to Him means: He is exalted, in all these states, above likeness and modality. Al-Tha'labi said: the matter is, as it is narrated in the Torah: "Allah came from Sinai, rose from Se'ir, and manifested Himself from Paran," meaning: His commands appeared through His prophets in these states. The pronoun in "innahu" refers to the matter and the affair. Al-Tabari said: the people of Kufa call it "al-majhūla" (the unknown). Allah the Exalted comforted him with His attributes: the might with which there is no fear, and the wisdom, meaning: there is no deficiency in His actions.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verses 10–12:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And cast your staff." But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in retreat and did not return. "O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence.﴾ ﴿Except for one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil—indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without disease. [This is] among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people. Indeed, they have been a defiantly disobedient people.﴾

Allah the Exalted commanded him with these two matters, training him in their use. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimated form being: "So Moses cast the staff," ﴿and when he saw it moving﴾. Some readers read "ra'āhā" (he saw it) with imala (a vowel inclination, imāla). "Al-jann" (the jinn/snake) means serpents, because they conceal themselves (tukhfī anfusahā), that is, they hide themselves. Another group said: "al-jann" means small serpents. Moses' staff became a serpent, a thu'bān (a large serpent), which is the great one. It was compared to al-jann only in the speed of its agitation, because small creatures are more active than large ones. On either view, Allah, blessed and exalted, created in the staff and changed its attributes and accidents, so it became a serpent. Al-Zuhrī and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "jaʾan" with a hamza.

When Moses, peace be upon him, perceived the terror of that sight, ﴿he turned back in retreat and did not return﴾. Mujāhid said: he did not return; Qatāda said: he did not look back.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"ʿAqqaba al-rajulu" means that a man turned away from a matter and then turned his body or face toward it, as if he had turned back on his heels. Allah called to him, giving him companionship and strengthening him for the matter: ﴿O Moses, do not fear﴾, for My messengers whom I have chosen for prophethood do not fear in My presence and with Me. Moses, peace be upon him, then took the serpent and his staff returned; then it became a habit for him.

People differed concerning the exception in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Except for one who wronged﴾. Muqātil and others said: the exception is continuous (muttaṣil), and it concerns the prophets. Al-Ḥasan related that Allah, the Exalted, said to Moses: "I frightened you because of your killing of a soul." Al-Ḥasan also said: The prophets would sin and be punished, then they would sin—by Allah—and be punished, so how about us? Ibn Jurayj said: Allah does not frighten the prophets except because of a sin one of them has committed; if he commits it, He frightens him until He takes it from him. Many scholars said: none of mankind is known to have had a sin for them except what is related about Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā, peace be upon them both.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The scholars agreed that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected (maʿṣūmūn) from major sins and from those minor sins that are base (raḏāʾil), and they differed regarding what is beyond that. Perhaps al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj were pointing to what lies beyond that.

In the verse, on this interpretation, there is an ellipsis which brevity and eloquence required by leaving out its explicit statement; its estimated form is: "Whoever wronged and then substituted good after evil." Al-Farrāʾ and a group said: the exception is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), and it is a report about other than the prophets, as if he said: whoever among people wronged and then repented, indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful. Another group said: "illā" means "wa" (and).

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view has no basis. Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ and Zayd ibn Aslam read: "Alā man ẓalama" as an opening particle (istiftāḥ). His words, the Exalted: ﴿then substituted good﴾ mean: righteous deed accompanied by repentance. This verse implies the certainty of forgiveness for the penitent. The people agreed on this regarding repentance from polytheism (shirk), while the People of the Sunna held that regarding the penitent from sins, he is under Allah's will like one who persists; but hope predominates for the penitent and fear for the one who persists. His words, the Exalted: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 48] encompass all, both the penitent and the persistent, and there is no difference between the polytheist and others; for otherwise it would nullify its benefit, since shirk is forgiven for the penitent, and what is less than it is likewise on their interpretation. So what is the benefit of the distinction in the verse? This argument is binding, so reflect on it. It is related from Abū ʿAmr that he read: "ḥasanan baʿda sūʾ" with fatḥa on the ḥāʾ and the sīn, and this is the reading of Mujāhid and Ibn Abī Layla. Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-Iṣbahānī read: "ḥusnā" on the pattern of fuʿlā.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to put his hand into the opening of his robe, because it had no sleeve, as Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. Mujāhid said: a woolen garment reaching to part of his hand. "Al-jayb" is the opening in a garment for a person's head. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verses 10–12:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And cast your staff." But when he saw it moving as if it were a snake, he turned back in retreat and did not return. "O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence.﴾ ﴿Except for one who wrongs and then substitutes good after evil—indeed, I am Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without disease. Allah the Exalted commanded him with these two matters, training him in their use. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimated form being: "So Moses cast the staff," ﴿and when he saw it moving﴾. Some readers read "ra'āhā" (he saw it) with imala (a vowel inclination, imāla). Moses' staff became a serpent, a thu'bān (a large serpent), which is the great one. It was compared to al-jann only in the speed of its agitation, because small creatures are more active than large ones. On either view, Allah, blessed and exalted, created in the staff and changed its attributes and accidents, so it became a serpent. Al-Zuhrī and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "jaʾan" with a hamza.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"ʿAqqaba al-rajulu" means that a man turned away from a matter and then turned his body or face toward it, as if he had turned back on his heels. Moses, peace be upon him, then took the serpent and his staff returned; then it became a habit for him.

People differed concerning the exception in His words, the Exalted: ﴿Except for one who wronged﴾. Muqātil and others said: the exception is continuous (muttaṣil), and it concerns the prophets. Al-Ḥasan related that Allah, the Exalted, said to Moses: "I frightened you because of your killing of a soul." Al-Ḥasan also said: The prophets would sin and be punished, then they would sin—by Allah—and be punished, so how about us? Ibn Jurayj said: Allah does not frighten the prophets except because of a sin one of them has committed; if he commits it, He frightens him until He takes it from him. Many scholars said: none of mankind is known to have had a sin for them except what is related about Yaḥyā ibn Zakariyyā, peace be upon them both.

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The scholars agreed that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected (maʿṣūmūn) from major sins and from those minor sins that are base (raḏāʾil), and they differed regarding what is beyond that. Perhaps al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj were pointing to what lies beyond that.

In the verse, on this interpretation, there is an ellipsis which brevity and eloquence required by leaving out its explicit statement; its estimated form is: "Whoever wronged and then substituted good after evil." Al-Farrāʾ and a group said: the exception is disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), and it is a report about other than the prophets, as if he said: whoever among people wronged and then repented, indeed I am Forgiving and Merciful. Another group said: "illā" means "wa" (and).

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view has no basis. Abū Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ and Zayd ibn Aslam read: "Alā man ẓalama" as an opening particle (istiftāḥ). Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verses 13–14:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿So when Our signs came to them, clear to see, they said, "This is plain magic." And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance. So see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾

The pronoun in His words ﴿came to them﴾ refers to Pharaoh and his people. "Mubsira" (clear to see) means: with it is sight (ibsar) and clarity. On this basis is the idiom of their saying: "a day that fasts" (nahar sa'im), and "a night that stands and sleeps" (layl qa'im wa-na'im). Qatada and al-Hasan recited "mabsara" with a fatha on the mim and the sad.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ is that disbelief occurred out of obstinacy. This is a question on which there are two opinions: can it happen or not? One group permitted it and said: it is possible that a man knows the truth but denies it out of obstinacy and dies upon both his knowledge and his denial, so he is in the ruling of the eternal disbeliever. They said: this is the ruling of Iblis, and the ruling of Huyayy ibn Akhtab and his brother, according to what has been narrated about them.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Even if this example is opposed, let it be supposed that there is a person for whom this is possible. Another group said: it is not sound, for two reasons. The first is that this cannot occur from a sane person. The second is that knowledge requires that it settle in the heart, and that is faith; the ruling of disbelief does not attach to it unless disbelief settles in the heart, and the joining of two opposites in one place is not sound. They said: what resembles this is that the knower who denies has that knowledge removed at the time of his death and disbelief takes its place.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

What appears to me regarding this verse and what is like it is that when these disbelievers looked at the signs of Moses, their own words gave them away: "This is not within the power of humans," and certainty of their being from Allah the Exalted arose in them. Then envy overcame them in the midst of that, and they clung to conjectures that they were magic and other things, until that certainty was removed or pushed away. Its ruling is the ruling of one whose certainty has been removed, regarding the obligation of their punishment.

"Zulman" (out of wrongdoing) means: without any entitlement to denial. "Al-'uluw" (arrogance) on earth is the gravest affliction for the one who seeks it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is the abode of the Hereafter; We grant it to those who do not desire haughtiness upon the earth or corruption﴾ [al-Qasas: 83]. Then the Exalted One expressed His wonder at the end of the corrupters, the people of Pharaoh, and the evil of their final state when they denied Moses. In this there is an illustration for the disbelievers of Quraysh, since they were corrupters and arrogant. Ibn Thabbat, Talha and al-A'mash recited "wa-'uliyyan," and Abu 'Amr al-Dani related from them and from Aban ibn Taghlib that they gave the 'ayn of "'ilyyan" a kasra.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verse 15–17:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman. And they said: "All praise is for Allah, who has favoured us above many of His believing servants."﴾ ﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud. He said: "O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds, and we have been given of everything. Indeed, this is the clear bounty."﴾ ﴿And for Sulayman were gathered his soldiers of the jinn and the mankind and the birds, and they were marshalled in ranks.﴾

This is the beginning of a narrative containing unseen matters and lessons, and it is not an example for Quraysh. Dawud, peace be upon him, was from the Children of Israel and was a king. Sulayman, peace be upon him, inherited his kingdom and his rank of prophethood, meaning that this passed to him after the death of his father. It is called "inheritance" metaphorically (tajawwuz), and this is like their saying: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets." The literal sense of inheritance is in wealth, and the prophets do not bequeath their wealth, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance," meaning that this is the action and practice of the prophets, peace be upon them, even though some of them did leave their wealth as an inheritance, such as Zakariyya, peace be upon him, according to the most well-known opinion concerning him. This is like when you say: "We, the company of Muslims, are occupied only with worship," meaning that this is the action of the majority. From this is what Sibawayh related: "We, the company of Arabs, are the most generous of people toward the guest."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have been taught the speech of the birds﴾ is an announcement of the blessing of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, upon them both, in that they understood from the sounds of the birds the meanings that are in their souls. This is like what our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ used to hear, the sounds of the stones greeting him with peace. Sulayman, peace be upon him, related from the nightingale that it said: "You have eaten half a date, so let the world perish," and many other things of this kind. Qatada, al-Sha'bi and others said: this matter was only with regard to birds, and the ant is a bird since it may have wings. al-Sha'bi said: and that ant was likewise one with two wings. A group said: rather it was in all animals. He mentioned the birds only because they were a host of Sulayman's soldiers, screening the sun from him and being employed by him in dispatching affairs, so they were singled out for their frequent involvement. And because the matter of the rest of the animals (p-525) is rare and not as frequently recurring as the matter of the birds. The ant is a clever, strong, and very perceptive animal; it stores provisions, splits grain into two pieces so that it does not sprout, splits coriander into four pieces because it sprouts when divided in halves, and it eats half of what it has gathered in its year and keeps the rest for a period.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and we have been given of everything﴾ means: it is suitable for us and we wish for it, and it is not meant in its generality. Then he repeated the thanks of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted.

Then the Exalted related the condition of Sulayman, saying: ﴿And for Sulayman were gathered﴾, i.e., were assembled. People differed greatly regarding the quantity of Sulayman's soldiers, and I did not wish to mention it because it is not authentic. However, the correct view is that his kingdom was great; it filled the earth, and the whole inhabited world submitted to him. His throne was carried by his troops of the jinn and mankind, and the birds shaded him from the sun and he dispatched them on affairs. So he had a place of distinction on the Great Throne. The meaning of "they were marshalled" (yuza'un) is: their first is held back until their last joins them, and they are restrained. Qatada said: each category had its marshals in their ranks and their places around the throne and on the earth when they walked over it—for there was a time when he would travel across the earth. From this is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri when he assumed the judgeship of Basra: "The judge must have guards (wazaʿa)." From this is the saying of Abu Quhafa when the slave-girl described to him, on the day of the conquest, that she saw a black figure in front of him, a horseman who had advanced from the line, and he said to her: "That is the wazi' (one who restrains)." From this is the saying of the poet:

"When I rebuked white hair for my youth, and you said: 'Will I not awaken, while the white hair is restraining?'"

That is: restraining.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verse 15–17:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And We certainly gave knowledge to Dawud and Sulayman. And they said: "All praise is for Allah, who has favoured us above many of His believing servants."﴾ ﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud. He said: "O people, we have been taught the speech of the birds, and we have been given of everything. Indeed, this is the clear bounty."﴾ ﴿And for Sulayman were gathered his soldiers of the jinn and the mankind and the birds, and they were marshalled in ranks.﴾

This is the beginning of a narrative containing unseen matters and lessons, and it is not an example for Quraysh. Dawud, peace be upon him, was from the Children of Israel and was a king. Sulayman, peace be upon him, inherited his kingdom and his rank of prophethood, meaning that this passed to him after the death of his father. It is called "inheritance" metaphorically (tajawwuz), and this is like their saying: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets." The literal sense of inheritance is in wealth, and the prophets do not bequeath their wealth, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "We, the company of prophets, do not leave inheritance," meaning that this is the action and practice of the prophets, peace be upon them, even though some of them did leave their wealth as an inheritance, such as Zakariyya, peace be upon him, according to the most well-known opinion concerning him. This is like when you say: "We, the company of Muslims, are occupied only with worship," meaning that this is the action of the majority. From this is what Sibawayh related: "We, the company of Arabs, are the most generous of people toward the guest."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We have been taught the speech of the birds﴾ is an announcement of the blessing of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, upon them both, in that they understood from the sounds of the birds the meanings that are in their souls. This is like what our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ used to hear, the sounds of the stones greeting him with peace. Sulayman, peace be upon him, related from the nightingale that it said: "You have eaten half a date, so let the world perish," and many other things of this kind. Qatada, al-Sha'bi and others said: this matter was only with regard to birds, and the ant is a bird since it may have wings. al-Sha'bi said: and that ant was likewise one with two wings. A group said: rather it was in all animals. He mentioned the birds only because they were a host of Sulayman's soldiers, screening the sun from him and being employed by him in dispatching affairs, so they were singled out for their frequent involvement. And because the matter of the rest of the animals (p-525) is rare and not as frequently recurring as the matter of the birds. The ant is a clever, strong, and very perceptive animal; it stores provisions, splits grain into two pieces so that it does not sprout, splits coriander into four pieces because it sprouts when divided in halves, and it eats half of what it has gathered in its year and keeps the rest for a period.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and we have been given of everything﴾ means: it is suitable for us and we wish for it, and it is not meant in its generality. Then he repeated the thanks of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted.

Then the Exalted related the condition of Sulayman, saying: ﴿And for Sulayman were gathered﴾, i.e., were assembled. People differed greatly regarding the quantity of Sulayman's soldiers, and I did not wish to mention it because it is not authentic. However, the correct view is that his kingdom was great; it filled the earth, and the whole inhabited world submitted to him. His throne was carried by his troops of the jinn and mankind, and the birds shaded him from the sun and he dispatched them on affairs. So he had a place of distinction on the Great Throne. The meaning of "they were marshalled" (yuza'un) is: their first is held back until their last joins them, and they are restrained. Qatada said: each category had its marshals in their ranks and their places around the throne and on the earth when they walked over it—for there was a time when he would travel across the earth. From this is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri when he assumed the judgeship of Basra: "The judge must have guards (wazaʿa)." From this is the saying of Abu Quhafa when the slave-girl described to him, on the day of the conquest, that she saw a black figure in front of him, a horseman who had advanced from the line, and he said to her: "That is the wazi' (one who restrains)." From this is the saying of the poet:

"When I rebuked white hair for my youth, and you said: 'Will I not awaken, while the white hair is restraining?'"

That is: restraining.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verse 18–19:

Allah's words, the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants, an ant said, "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his soldiers crush you while they do not perceive."﴾ ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her saying, and said, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have blessed me and upon my parents, and to do righteous deeds that please You, and admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."﴾

The apparent meaning of this verse is that Solomon, peace be upon him, and his soldiers were walking on the earth, and therefore the crushing of the ants [by their descent into the valley of the ants] is plausible. It is also possible that they were on the throne carried by the wind, and the ants sensed their descent into the valley of the ants. [As for the valley of the ants, it was said to be in al-Sham, and it was said to be at the far end of Yemen; it is known among the Arabs and mentioned in their poetry.]

Abu 'Amr inclined the waw in "wadi" (the valley), while the rest pronounced it with full emphasis (fakhkham). Ibn Abi Ishaq recited with the inclination (imala). Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman recited, on the authority of his father, "al-namlu" with a damma on the mim, like "al-shamsu," and [qalat namlah] also with a damma, like "sumrah." It is also narrated from him that the nun and the mim of "al-namli" were both given a damma. Nawf al-Bakali said: that ant was the size of a fly. Another group said: rather, they were small.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What is said about this is that the ant's proportion relative to that creation was like the proportion of this ant relative to us, so it is possible that the whole creation was more perfect. This ant spoke this meaning—which only this expression suits—in a speech that the ants understood from her, and Solomon, peace be upon him, heard it despite the distance, and the address came as to one who understands, because she commanded them with what is commanded to one who understands. It is narrated that he was at a distance of three miles (p-527), so he smiled at her words. Smiling is the laughter of the prophets in most of their affairs; nothing other than it befits them.

His laughter was from joy, and it was disputed: at what? One group said: at the blessing of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, in enabling him to hear and to understand and the like. Another group said: at the report of the ant concerning him and his soldiers, in that she cleared them of intentionally doing an ugly act, so she made the crushing something they did without perceiving.

Shahr ibn Hawshab recited "maskanikum" with a sukun on the sin, in the singular. In the Codex of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, it is "masakinukunna." The majority of reciters recited "la yahtimannakum" with a shaddah on the nun and a sukun on the ha'. Abu 'Amr, and in a narration from Ubayda, recited "la yahtimannakum" with a sukun on the nun; this is the recitation of Ibn Abi Ishaq. Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' recited "la yuhattimannakum" with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the ha', a kasra on the ta' and its shaddah, and a shaddah on the nun. Also from him: "la yahittimannakum" with a fatha on the ya', a kasra on the ha' and the ta' and its shaddah. Al-A'mash and Talhah recited "la yahtimkum," lightened, without a nun. In the Codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "la yahtimannakum" with the nun preceding the kaf lightened.

"Dahikan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "dahikan" [i.e., "dahkan"], which is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar) [governed by a deleted verb indicated by "tabassama," as if he said "daḥika daḥikan"; this is the position of the author of the Kitab (Sibawayh), or it is accusative by "tabassama" itself, since it carries the meaning of "daḥika" (laughed)].

Then Solomon, peace be upon him, invoked his Lord that Allah, the Exalted, would help him and free him to give thanks for His blessing; this is the meaning of inspiring gratitude (iza' al-shukr). The rest of the verse is clear.

(p-528)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verses 20–23:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And he inspected the birds and said, "Why do I not see the hoopoe? Or is he among the absent?"﴾ ﴿"I will surely punish him with a severe punishment, or slaughter him, or he must bring me a clear authority."﴾ ﴿But he remained not far off and said, "I have encompassed [knowledge] that you have not encompassed, and I have come to you from Sheba with certain information."﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I found a woman ruling over them, and she has been given of all things, and she has a great throne."﴾

The people have differed concerning the meaning of "his inspecting the birds." One group said: this is in accordance with what the concern for the affairs of the kingdom requires, and attentiveness to every part of it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of the verse is that he inspected all the birds. Another group said: rather, he inspected the birds because the sun had entered upon the king from the place where the hoopoe was when it was absent, so this was the reason for inspecting the birds, to ascertain from where the sun had entered. 'Abdullah ibn Salam said: he sought the hoopoe only because he needed to know where water was located beneath the surface of the earth, since he had descended into a desert in which water was denied to him; and because the hoopoe could see the inside and outside of the earth, as if it were transparent to it, and it used to inform Sulayman, peace be upon him, of the place of water; then the jinn would extract it in a short time, the surface of the earth being flayed off it as a sheep is skinned. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, as narrated from Abu Salam and others. And in the book of al-Naqqash it is said: the hoopoe was an engineer. It is related that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq heard Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, say this, and said to him: "Stop, O one who stops at nothing! How can the hoopoe see the inside of the earth when it does not see the snare when it falls into it?" Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said to him: "When the decree comes, sight becomes blind." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the birds used to visit Sulayman, peace be upon him, every day, each kind in a known turn, and he missed the hoopoe.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Why do I not see﴾ — the intended meaning is that the hoopoe was absent, but he took the necessary consequence of its absence, which is that he does not see it, and so he asked, in the manner of reproach, about the necessary consequence. This is a kind of concision, and the interrogative in his saying "Why for me" takes the place of the alif which "am" requires. Then he (peace be upon him) threatened it with punishment. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj that his punishment of the bird would be by plucking all its feathers; Yazid ibn Ruman said: its wing; and it is related from Wahb that it would be by plucking part of it and leaving a portion. And "sultan" means proof wherever it occurs in the Qur'an, as said by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ikrimah alone read: "li-ya'tiyanni" with two nuns. Sulayman, peace be upon him, did this to the hoopoe alone, out of severity toward the disobedient, and because of its neglect of its turn and its rank.

The majority of readers read: "fa-makuta" with a damma on the kaf; 'Asim alone read: "fa-makatha" with a fatha on it. Its meaning in both readings is: he remained. The fatha on the kaf is better, because it is the language of the Qur'an in His saying "makithin" (remaining), since it is from "makatha" with a fatha on the kaf; and if it were from "makuta" with a damma on the kaf, its plural would be "makith." The pronoun in "makatha" may refer to Sulayman, peace be upon him, or to the hoopoe. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "fa-tamakkatha thumma ja'a fa-qala," and in the reading of Ubayy: "fa-tamakkatha thumma qala ahatta." His saying "ghayra ba'id," as in the codices of the majority, means by it time and duration. His saying "ahatu" means: I have known with complete knowledge that is not in your knowledge.

The readers differed concerning "Saba'," the majority read "Saba'in" with tanwin (nunation). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "Saba'" with a fatha on the hamza and without nunation. al-A'mash read "min Saba'in" with a kasra and without nunation. Ibn Habib related from al-Yazidi "Saba'" with a quiescent alif. Qanbal, from al-Nabbal, read with a quiescent hamza. The first is on the basis that it is the name of a man, and upon this is the saying of the poet:

"The comers and Taym on the heights of Saba' — the hide of buffaloes has bitten their necks."

And another said:

"From Saba', those present at Ma'arib..."

This is on the basis that it is a tribe, while the second is on the basis that it is a city, as said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. Both opinions have been stated. However, it has been related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, through the hadith of Farwa ibn Musayk and others, that "ten sons were born to him; six of them went to the right and four to the left," and this hadith was attributed to al-Zajjaj, and he blundered badly. The third is on the basis of indeclinability. The fourth and fifth are because of the succession of the seven vowel-movements, so it was made quiescent for lightness, due to the heaviness of successive movements. This reading is not built upon the first, but is either upon the second or the third. A group read without nunation on the basis of the construct (idafa), and a group read "bi-naba" with a long alif.

His saying: ﴿And she has been given of all things﴾ is hyperbole, meaning: of what a kingdom needs. Al-Hasan said: of all the affairs of the world. He described her throne as great in its form and in the rank of sovereignty. It is related from Nafi' that he paused at "'arsh," so "'azim" — on this reading — is connected to what follows. This woman is Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil, according to some of them; it was said: daughter of al-Qashrah; and it was said: her mother was a jinn. Some people have elaborated greatly on her stories with what I have seen, I have abridged it because it is not sound. What is necessarily implied by the verse is that she was specific to a woman who was made ruler over the cities of Yemen, possessed a great kingdom, and was a disbeliever from a disbelieving people.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 27, verses 24–28:**

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah. Satan has made their deeds seem fair to them and has averted them from the way, so they are not guided.﴾ ﴿Why do they not prostrate to Allah, who brings forth what is hidden in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you disclose?﴾ ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Lord of the Mighty Throne.﴾ ﴿[Solomon] said: "We shall see whether you have told the truth or whether you are among the liars."﴾ ﴿Go with this letter of mine and deliver it to them, then withdraw from them and see what they return.﴾

This nation worshipped the sun, because, as it is narrated, they were zindiqs (heretics). It has also been said that they were Magians who worshipped lights. As for His words, ﴿Why do they not prostrate﴾ up to His words, ﴿the Mighty Throne﴾, it is apparent that this is the speech of the hoopoe (al-hudhud). This is the view of Ibn Zayd and Ibn Ishaq. It is objected that the hoopoe was not addressed, so how could it speak on a matter of religious law? [It is possible that it is the speech of Solomon, when the hoopoe informed him about the people.] It is also possible that it is the speech of Allah, the Exalted, and thus it is an interjection between the two statements. This is the one that stands on careful reflection. The reading with the shaddah on "*alla*" (that is, *allā*) indicates that the speech belongs to the hoopoe, whereas the reading with the lightened form (*allā*, with the lam unstressed) rules this out and strengthens the other view, according to what has been heard. Let one reflect on this, if Allah wills.

The majority of the readers (qurra') read "*allā*", meaning "*lā yasjudū*" (that they do not prostrate). Thus "*an*" is in a position of accusative (naṣb) by way of substitution (badal) for "*a'mālahum*", or in a position of genitive (khafḍ) by way of substitution for "*al-sabīl*". Or the statement may be understood with the implied meaning "*li-allā yasjudū*" (so that they do not prostrate), in which case "*an*" is linked either to "*zayyana*" or to "*faṣaddahum*", and the lam that enters upon "*an*" enters upon an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu).

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Ja'far, al-Zuhri, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, al-Kisa'i and al-Husayn read "*alā yasjudū*" with the lam lightened. According to this reading, one may pause at "*fahum lā yahtadūn*" and begin with "*alā yasjudū*". Or, if one wishes, one may pause at "*alā yā*" and then begin with "*usjudū*" (prostrate!). Al-Kisa'i argued for this reading by saying that it has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that this is a place of prostration. If we take it as part of the hoopoe's speech, the meaning is: "Alā yā qawmi" (O my people, indeed) and similar. From this is the verse of the poet:

*Alā yā-slamī yā dāra Mayy 'alā al-bilā*
*wa lā zāla munhalan bi-jar'ā'ik al-qaṭru*

And like the saying of al-Akhtal:

*Alā yā-aslimī yā Hindu Hindu banī Badru* ***
*wa in kāna ḥayyānā 'adā ākhira al-dahri*

And from this is the saying of another:

*Alā yā-sma' a'iẓuka bi-khuṭbatin* ***
*fa-qultu sami'nā fa-nṭiqī wa aṣībī*

[p. 533] The reading of the one who shaddahs "*allā*" may also be understood as expressing urging (taḥḍīḍ), with this call (nidā') supplied after it. This involves a considerable implied element (iḍmār), but it is sound. The alif is dropped as it is written in "*yā 'Īsā*" and "*yā qawmu*". Al-A'mash read "*halla yasjudūn*". In the codex of 'Abd Allah it is "*alā hal tasjudūn*" with the ta'. In the reading of Ubayy it is "*allā tasjudū*", also with the ta'.

"*Al-khab'*" means the hidden matters, and it derives from "*khabba'tu al-shay'*" (I hid the thing). The khab' of the sky is its rain, and the khab' of the earth is its treasures and plants. The word thereafter encompasses every hidden matter, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, interpreted it thus. Most people read "*al-khab'*" with a sukun on the ba' and with hamz. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "*al-khaba*" with a fatha on the ba' and without hamz. Ikrimah read "*al-khabā*" with a short alif. Sibawayh reported that some Arabs change the hamzah into an alif when it is fathah and preceded by a sukun, into a waw when it is ḍammah and preceded by a sukun, and into a yā' when it is kasrah and preceded by a sukun. Sibawayh gave as an example "*al-wathy*", and you say: "I saw *al-wathā*, this is *al-wathw*, and I was amazed at *al-wathy*." Likewise "*al-khabā*" comes in the accusative case, and you say: "I looked at [p. 534] *al-khabī*, and *al-khabw* pleased me." The majority of readers read "*wa yaʿlamu mā yukhfūna wa mā yuʿlinūna*" with the yā' of the third person.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This reading indicates that the verse is part of the speech of the hoopoe. Al-Kisa'i and 'Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "*wa ya'lamu mā tukhfūna wa mā tu'linūna*" with the ta' of the second person. This reading indicates that the verse is an address from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to the nation of Muhammad ﷺ. In the codex of Ibn Ka'b it is: "*allā tasjudū li-llāhi alladhī yakhruju al-khaba min al-samāwāti wa al-arḍi wa ya'lamu sirrakum wa mā tu'linūn*."

He singled out the Throne for mention in His words ﴿the Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾ because it is the greatest of created things, and all else is within it and in its grasp.

Then, Solomon, peace be upon him, postponed the matter of the hoopoe until it became clear to him what was true from what was false. So he deferred the matter by saying that he would examine it. He ordered a letter to be written, gave it to the hoopoe, and commanded it to deliver it to the people and then withdraw afterwards. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: He commanded it to withdraw as a matter of good manners, so that it might step aside in the manner in which one behaves with kings, meaning: "Remain nearby until you see their responses." He said: His words ﴿see what they return﴾ carry the sense of being placed before His words ﴿then withdraw﴾.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The coherence of the sequence of the speech is more evident: that is, "deliver it, then withdraw, and in the meantime look." He only intended to leave the matter to whatever judgment was in the letter, without the messenger staying with them and without pressing them. Nafi' read "*fa-alqihi*" with a kasrah on the ha'. A group read "*fa-alqihu*" with a ḍammah. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a prolonged vowel after the kasrah on the ha', and Warsh narrated from him a yā' after the ha' in connected speech. A group read it with a prolonged waw after the ḍammah. Al-Yazidi, from Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Hamzah, read "*fa-alqihi*" with a sukun on the ha'.

It is narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, concerning the stories of this verse, that the hoopoe arrived [p. 535] and cast the letter, passing beyond this queen the curtains of walls. It made for a window which Bilqis had made so that the sun might enter through it at its rising, for the purpose of her worshipping it. It entered through it and dropped the letter upon Bilqis, who, as is related, was sleeping. When she awoke she found it, and she was alarmed and thought that someone had entered upon her. Then she stood up and found her state as she had known it. She looked toward the window, intent upon the matter of the sun, and saw the hoopoe, and so she knew its affair. Then she gathered the people of her kingdom and its nobles, and addressed them with what comes after this.

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿She said: "O chiefs! Indeed, there has been delivered to me a noble letter."﴾ ﴿"It is from Sulayman, and it reads: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."﴾ ﴿"Do not exalt yourselves against me, but come to me in submission."﴾ ﴿She said: "O chiefs! Advise me in my affair; I would not decide a matter until you bear witness."﴾ ﴿They said: "We are possessors of strength and possessors of great might, but the command is yours, so consider what you will command."﴾ ﴿She said: "Indeed, when kings enter a town they corrupt it and make the most honored of its people abased. Thus do they do."﴾

In these verses there is an omission which the apparent wording indicates, its implied sense being: so she cast the letter, and she read it, and she gathered her realm's people for him. "Al-mala'" (the chiefs) are the notables of the people, who stand in for the whole. She described the letter as noble, either because it came from one great in her own estimation and in theirs, so she magnified it out of reverence for Sulayman, and this is the saying of Ibn Zayd; or because it was sealed with a signet, and it has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "The nobility of a letter is its seal." Or because she intended that it began with the name of Allah the Exalted, and the Prophet ﷺ has said: "Every speech that does not begin with the name of Allah the Exalted is deficient (ajdham)." Then she began describing to them what was in the letter. The wording may mean that the text of the letter was concise and eloquent, and so were the letters of the prophets, peace be upon them; he placed the heading first, which is the custom of people throughout time, then named Allah the Exalted, then commanded them not to exalt themselves over him in tyranny and disbelief, and to come to him in submission. It is also possible that she aimed at summarizing its meanings without its arrangement, so she informed them that it was from Sulayman and that its meaning was such-and-such.

Ubayy recited "wa-anna bismi Allah" with a fatha on the hamza, a light nun, and without the ha'; Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited "annahu min" and "wa-annahu bismi Allah" with a fatha on the hamza in both; in the reading of 'Abdullah it is "wa-innahu min Sulayman" with an added waw. The phrase ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is a noble opening of far-reaching meaning, expressed in every language and in every law (shar').

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verses 35–37:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And indeed, I am going to send them a gift, and will wait to see with what the envoys return.﴾ ﴿So when he (the messenger) came to Sulayman, he said, "Will you provide me with wealth? What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you. Rather, it is you who rejoice in your gift."﴾ ﴿Return to them, for we will surely come to them with hosts they cannot resist, and we will surely drive them out from it in humiliation, and they will be debased.﴾

It is narrated that Bilqis said to her people: "I will test this man with a gift, in which I will give him precious wealth, and I will test him with matters of the kingdom. If he is a worldly king, wealth will please him, and we will deal with him according to that. But if he is a prophet, wealth will not please him, and he will insist on matters of religion. In that case, it is fitting that we believe in him and follow his religion." So she sent him a great gift, and some people have exaggerated in detailing it, but I have chosen to abridge that because it is not authentic. It is also narrated that she tested his knowledge by sending him a cup and saying to him: "Fill it for me with what is neither from the earth nor from the sky." She also sent him a pearl with a hole bored crookedly in it, saying: "Thread its string without a human or a jinn coming near it," and sent another that was not perforated, saying: "Bore a hole in this one, other than humans and jinn." So Sulayman, peace be upon him, filled the cup with sweat from the mountain, the string was passed through the pearl by a worm, and the pearl was pierced by a termite. Sulayman, peace be upon him, responded regarding the rejection of the gift with what is in the verse. He expressed "the envoys" with "came" (jā'a) and with his saying "return" (irji') when he intended by it "the messenger," which applies to the plural and singular, feminine and masculine. Ibn Mas'ud read: "When they came to Sulayman" (jā'ū), and read "return" (irji'ū). Sulayman's threat to them is linked to their persistence in disbelief. Mujahid also mentioned that in her gift she sent a large number of slaves, boys and girls, and made their attire uniform, and she tested him by separating them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not a test in a matter of such gravity.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "Atumiddūnanī" (أتُمِدُّونَنِي) with two nūns and a yā' in pause and continuation. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read: "Atumiddūnan" (أتُمِدُّونَنِ) without a yā', both in pause and continuation. Hamza read: "Atumiddūnnī" (أتُمِدُّونِّي) with a doubled nūn and the yā' retained. 'Asim read: "Fa-mā ātāni-llāh" (فَما آتانِ اللهُ) with a kasra on the nūn and no yā'. A group read: "Ātāniyi" (آتانِيِ) with a sukun yā'. Abu 'Amr and Nafi' read: "Ātāniya" (آتانِيَ) with a fatha yā'.

Then he threatened them with hosts, with overpowering, and with expulsion, meaning: if they do not submit. 'Abdullah read: [lā qibala lahum bihim] (لا قِبَلَ لَهم بِهِمْ), using the plural pronoun referring to the hosts. "Lā qibala" (لا قِبَلَ) means: they have no capacity and no ability to resist.

The first view is more sound.

It is related that her throne was of gold and silver, adorned with jewels and rubies, and that it was inside seven chambers, upon which were seven locks.

A group said: rather, it was Sulayman (peace be upon him) himself, and the address, in this interpretation, is to the ʿifrit, when he said: ﴿I will bring it to you before you rise from your place.﴾ It was said: as if Sulayman (peace be upon him) found this slow, so he said to him, in a way of belittling him: ﴿I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you.﴾ The one who holds this view argued from Sulayman's saying (peace be upon him): ﴿This is from the bounty of my Lord﴾, and this view was also argued against by its opposite, since in both matters there is a bounty from Allah, the Exalted, upon Sulayman. On the earlier views, the address is to Sulayman (peace be upon him). The word "ātīka" may be a future verb, and it may be an active participle. There is an omission in the speech, its estimated form being: he called upon the name of Allah, the Exalted, and the throne came by the power of Allah, the Exalted. When Sulayman saw it settled beside him, he began to thank his Lord's blessing with an expression containing instruction for mankind, which is open to being followed and borrowed from. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "Shall I give thanks for the throne and its being brought, or shall I be ungrateful, seeing one lower than me in this world who is more knowledgeable than me?" The governing element of the adverbial phrase appears in his saying "mustaqirran" (settled), and this is what is always estimated in every adverbial phrase that occurs here explicitly, and there is no example of its like in the Book of Allah, the Exalted. The remainder of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verses 41–44:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿He said: "Disguise her throne for her; we shall see whether she is guided or is among those who are not guided."﴾ ﴿So when she came, it was said: "Is your throne like this?" She said: "It is as if it were it. And we were given knowledge before her, and we were Muslims."﴾ ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah averted her, for she was from a disbelieving people.﴾ ﴿It was said to her: "Enter the palace." And when she saw it she thought it was a pool of water, and she bared her shins. He said: "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass." She said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾

Sulayman intended by this "disguising" (al-tankir) a test by which he could distinguish her and see her (judgment), and to add to the strangeness (al-i'rab) for her. A group has related that the jinn sensed from Sulayman, or suspected of him, that he might marry Bilqis, so they disliked that, and they accused her before him of being neither intelligent nor discerning, and that her leg was like the hoof of a beast. So he tested her intellect (aqlaha) and her discernment by the disguising of her throne, and he tested the matter of her leg by the matter of the palace, so that she would uncover her shin in his presence. Abu Haywa recited "tanzuru" (تَنْظُرُ) with a damma on the ra'.

The disguising of the throne means altering its description and concealing part of it, and the like. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said: its disguising was by adding to it and subtracting from it. This objection arises: according to this view, she should have said "It is not it," and would have been truthful. Her saying "It is as if it were it" is an eloquent evasion (tahharruz fasih); similar to it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿as if he were a close friend﴾ [Fussilat: 34]. Al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: they confused her, so she confused them. Had they said, "Is this your throne?" she would have said, "Yes." In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: "So they disguised her throne, and looked at what her answer would be when asked about it. So when she came, it was said: 'Is your throne like this?'" Sulayman, peace be upon him, said at that: ﴿And we were given knowledge before her﴾, the verse, and this from him was by way of enumerating the blessing of Allah the Exalted upon him and upon his fathers.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And what she used to worship besides Allah averted her﴾, the verse, it may be that it is from the saying of the Prophet of Allah Sulayman, peace be upon him, and it may be that it is from the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, informing Muhammad ﷺ. The "averter" (al-sadd) is what she used to worship, i.e., from faith and the like. Al-Rummani said: from perceiving the throne, because the believer is perceptive and alert while the disbeliever is wicked. Or the averter may be Sulayman, peace be upon him; this was said by al-Tabari. Or the averter may be Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Since "sadda-ha" means "prevented her," it is transitive without a preposition on this interpretation; otherwise it is only transitive with "an" (from). The majority of readers recited "innaha" with a kasra on the hamza; Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "annaha" with a fatha on the hamza, and it is on the estimate: "That is because she..." or as a substitution (badal) for "ma," as said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

When Bilqis arrived, Sulayman, peace be upon him, commanded the jinn, and they made for him a palace (sarh), which is a flat roof in a courtyard without a ceiling; they made it built like a cistern, filled with water, in which he placed fish and frogs, and it was covered with transparent glass. Thus it came as a palace (sarh). Also, sarh is every high building, and all of this derives from tasrih, which is clear, extensive proclamation. In its middle was placed a seat (kursi) for Sulayman. When Bilqis reached it, it was said to her: "Enter to the Prophet ﷺ." She saw the expanse of water, was frightened, and thought that he intended her drowning; she marvelled that his seat was upon the water, and she saw what alarmed her, and she had no choice but to comply with the command, so she uncovered her shins. Sulayman saw her shins, sound from what the jinn had claimed, except that they were thick with hair. When she reached this limit, Sulayman, peace be upon him, said to her: ﴿Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth with glass.﴾ "Al-mumarrad" is that which is scraped and smooth; from it comes "al-amrad" (the beardless youth), and "al-shajara al-marda'" (the leafless tree), which has no leaves on it. Al-mumarrad also means "elongated," and from it the fortress is called "Marid." At that, Bilqis yielded, submitted, and accepted Islam, and acknowledged against herself wrongdoing. It is related that Sulayman, peace be upon him, married her at that time and settled her in al-Sham; this was said by al-Dahhak. Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said in the book of al-Naqqash: he married her and returned her to her kingdom in Yemen, and he would visit her on the wind once a month; she bore him a son whom she named Dawud, who died during his lifetime. "Ma'a" is an adverb (zarf); and it has been said it is a particle (harf) built on fatha. As for when its 'ayn is sukun, there is no disagreement that it is a particle that came for a meaning.

Ibn Kathir alone, in one narration (of al-Ikhrit), recited: "'an sa'iqiha" with a hamza. Abu 'Ali said: it is weak; and likewise the hamza is weak in Qunbul's recitation: "yakshifu 'an sa'q." As for hamzating "bis-sawq" and "'ala sawqihi," it is a well-known dialect in hamzating a waw preceded by a damma; Abu 'Ali related that Abu Hayya al-Numayri would hamzate every waw preceded by a damma, and he recited:

"Ahabbu al-mu'qadani ilayka mu'sa..."

Its justification is that the damma stands upon the waw, since there is no barrier between them. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "'an rijliha" (her foot). It is related that when Sulayman, peace be upon him, wanted the hair of her shins removed, he feared using a razor on her, and it was said that she had said: "Iron has never touched me," so he commanded the jinn to act gently in removing it, and they made depilatory cream (nura), which had not existed among the nations before.

These matters that Sulayman, peace be upon him, did — the driving of the throne, the making of the palace, and other things — he intended by them to outdo her in strangeness, just as she had previously followed the way of the kings of this world in that she sent servant-girls and boys, and proposed tests concerning the cup and the two pearls.

It is related that when Sulayman, peace be upon him, wanted the hair of her shins removed, he feared using a razor on her, and it was said that she had said: "Iron has never touched me," so he commanded the jinn to act gently in removing it, and they made depilatory cream (nura), which had not existed among the nations before.

These matters that Sulayman, peace be upon him, did — the driving of the throne, the making of the palace, and other things — he intended by them to outdo her in strangeness, just as she had previously followed the way of the kings of this world in that she sent servant-girls and boys, and proposed tests concerning the cup and the two pearls.

This verse is an illustration (tamthil) directed at Quraysh. The word "an" in His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿an u'budu Allah﴾ (that worship Allah) may be interpretive (mufassira), and it may be in the position of a accusative (nasb), the implied meaning being: bi-an u'budu Allah (with the worship of Allah).

By "two groups" (fariqan) He means: those who believed in Salih and those who disbelieved in him. Their "dispute" (ikhtisamuhum) is their mutual contention, and God, blessed and exalted, mentioned this in Surat al-A'raf.

Then Salih, peace be upon him, dealt gently with his people and was tender with them in address. He made them stand before their error in seeking hastened punishment, which would necessitate their destruction, and then urged them towards what is easier than that and more conducive to good, namely faith, seeking forgiveness and hoping for mercy. At that, they answered with a base (safsaf) statement, its meaning being: "We have taken an omen from you." The exegetes said: they were in a drought, so they attributed it to Salih, peace be upon him. The origin of tiyara (divination by omen) is what the people of ignorance recognized of observing birds (zajr al-tayr). The Arabs compared what occurs to a person with what flies, until it happened; what befalls a person in a fright or the like was called a "bird" (ta'ir). From this is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [al-Isra: 13]. Salih addressed them with a clear statement of the truth: "Your bird is with Allah," meaning: your lot, according to your claim and your naming, and it is in reality your portion of punishment or exemption, which is with Allah, exalted be He, and by His decree and His measure. Rather, you are a people who are being tested (takhtabarun). This is one of the aspects of fitna. It is also possible that it means: "Rather, you are a people who are infatuated with your desires (tawla'un bi-shahawatikum)." This is a meaning for which people have commonly used the word fitna, and from it is your saying: "Fulan was seduced (futina) by Fulan." Evidence for this is abundant.

God Almighty says:

﴿And in the city there were nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not reform.﴾ ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by Allah that we will surely attack him and his family by night, and then we will surely say to his heir, 'We did not witness the destruction of his family, and indeed we are truthful.'"﴾ ﴿And they schemed a scheme, and We schemed a scheme, while they were unaware.﴾ ﴿So see how was the outcome of their scheme: that We destroyed them and their people, all of them.﴾

In this verse Allah mentions nine men who were among the notables of the people, the most powerful and the wealthiest of them. They were people of disbelief and many sins, and the general sum of their affair was that they spread corruption in the land and did not reform. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "It reached me that they used to clip dinars and dirhams."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is close to the narration that is reported: "Clipping dinars and dirhams is among the corruption in the land." The "madinah" (city) here is the gathering place and town of Thamud. The "rahT" (a group of men) is among the nouns of collective plurality for a small number, namely ten and fewer than that. "Nine men" is like saying "nine men" (rijal). These mentioned people were the companions of Qidar ibn Salif, the one who hamstrung the she-camel. What was mentioned of their names has been discussed in another place.

As for Allah's words "taqasamu" (swear to one another), al-Tabari related that it may be a past verb in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as if he said: "swearing to one another" or "swearing to one another by Allah." Their statement "we will surely attack him" is then an oath. This interpretation is supported by the reading of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), in which it is "wa la yaslihun, taqasamu" without "qalu." It is also possible, and this is the interpretation of the majority, that "taqasamu" is an imperative verb, as some of them advised others to swear together upon this act with a pledge. In that case "taqasamu" is their statement according to this interpretation. These words that indicate an oath or an answer to an oath are answered with the lam (the lam of response) even if no explicit oath has preceded, so the lam in "la-nubayyitannahu" is the answer to that.

The majority of readers recited "linubayyitannahu" and "thumma la-naqulunnahu" with the nun in both. Al-Hasan, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited with the ta' in both and with a damma on the ta' and the lam, in the form of address, meaning: "address one another with this." Mujahid and Humayd ibn Qays recited with the ya' in both, in the form of narration. In this case Allah has mentioned the meaning they intended, not according to the wording of their speech.

It is also narrated concerning this verse that when these nine were in the first part of the three days after the slaughter of the she-camel, and Salih, peace be upon him, had informed them of the coming of the punishment, these nine agreed and swore an oath to come to the house of Salih at night and kill him and his family who were closest to him. They said: "If he is lying in his threat, we will have inflicted upon him what he deserves; and if he is truthful, we will have hastened him before us and healed our souls." The narrator said: "They came and hid for this purpose in a cave near his house." It is narrated that a rock fell upon them and crushed them all, and it is also narrated that the cave closed over them and they perished in it when their people perished. Each group did not know what happened to the other. They had based their plan on denying the matter, relying on the kinship of Salih, whom they thought might be angered on his behalf. This is their scheme. "Makr" (scheming) is like deception, and Allah, blessed and exalted, named their punishment by the name of their sin. This is a common usage, and among it is the verse ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15], and other examples.

The majority recited "muhlak" with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the lam. 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, recited with a fatha on both, and it is narrated from him that he recited with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the lam.

"Al-'aqibah" (the outcome) is a state that the beginning requires and leads to. By "the family" (ahl) is meant everyone who believed with him, as al-Hasan said. The majority of readers recited "innã dammarnahum" with a kasra on the alif (innā), while 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "anna dammarnahum" with a fatha on the alif (anna), and this is the reading of al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq. So "kana" (was), according to the reading with the kasra on the alif, is complete (tammah, meaning it needs no predicate). If it is considered incomplete (naqisah, meaning it requires a predicate), then its predicate is omitted, or the predicate is "kayfa" (how) placed first, because the opening of the sentence belongs to it. According to this view, "unzur" (look) does not govern "kayfa," but it governs the position of the whole clause. With the fatha on the alif, "kana" is incomplete and its predicate is "anna," though it is possible that the predicate is "kayfa," and "anna" is then a substitute (badal, apposition) for "al-'aqibah." It is also possible that "kana" is complete and "anna" is a substitute for "al-'aqibah." The implied question was framed with "kayfa" about the clause of His words: ﴿the outcome of their scheme was that We destroyed them﴾. Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "an dammarnahum," and this reading supports the fatha in "anna."

The rain that fell upon them was stones of sijjil, which destroyed all of them. This verse is the basis for those jurists who hold that stoning is the punishment for sodomy (liwat), and it is a support for them, because God punished them for their disbelief in Him and sent stones upon them for their disobedience. He did not analogize this ruling to fornication (zina), so as to take into account the condition of ihsan (marriage or chastity). Rather, Malik and others said: both are stoned in sodomy, whether they were married (ahsana) or not. The Prophet (ﷺ) only reported: "Kill the one who does it and the one it is done to," and those who held that both should be stoned did so on the basis of this verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verse 59–61:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿Say: "All praise is due to Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen. Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?"﴾ ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth, and sent down for you water from the sky, and with it caused to grow gardens of joyous beauty, whereas it was not for you to cause their trees to grow? Is there a god with Allah? Nay, but they are a people who ascribe equals (to Him).﴾ ﴿Is not He who made the earth a stable place, and made rivers within it, and made for it firm mountains, and placed between the two seas a barrier? Is there a god with Allah? Nay, but most of them do not know.﴾

Abu al-Samal recited "قُلَ الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ" (qula al-hamdu lillah) with a fathah on the lam, and likewise at the end of the surah. This (verse) is the beginning of an affirmation and confirmation addressed to Quraysh, and it also encompasses every accountable person among mankind, all of them. He opened this with praise and glorification of Him, and with peace upon His servants whom He chose for prophethood and faith. This wording is general to all of them from among the children of Adam, and it is as if this is the opening of a sermon for the aforementioned affirmation. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The servants upon whom peace is invoked are the companions of the Prophet ﷺ, whom He chose for His Prophet."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this specification there is a rebuke to the disbelievers of his time.

Al-Farra' said: The command to speak in this verse is directed to Lot, peace be upon him. The exegetes said: This is a mistake (ujma) on the part of al-Farra'.

Then, by way of rebuke, he confronted Quraysh and the Arabs with the point of difference between Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the idols and idols' stones. Most people recited "تُشْرِكُونَ" (tushrikun) with a ta' from above, while al-Mahdawi related from Abu 'Amr and 'Asim: "يُشْرِكُونَ" (yushrikun) with a ya' from below.

Regarding this preference expressed with the word "khayr" (better), there are several opinions. The first is that the preference occurred according to the belief of the polytheists, since they believed that their gods had some good in some respect. A group said: there is an elided genitive (mudaf) in both places, the sense being: "Is the Tawhid of Allah better, or the worship of what you associate?" Thus "ma" in this interpretation carries the meaning of "alladhi" (that which). Another group said: "ma" is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), and the elision of the mudaf occurs only at the first, its sense being: "Is the Tawhid of Allah better, or your shirk?" It was also said: "khayr" here is not an elative (af'al), but a verb-like usage, as you say "prayer is good" without comparison.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It has already been mentioned that these terms which encompass many meanings, such as "khayr" (good) and "sharr" (evil), or "hubb" (love) and the like, may be used for comparison between entirely different things, because entirely different things may share in them, even in a weak and remote respect. Furthermore, this is an affirmation, and the disputant affirms his opponent in order to alert him to his error and to bind him to restricting preference to one side and negating it from the other. We have covered this comprehensively earlier. A group said: the estimated sense of this verse is: "Is Allah possessor of good, or what you associate?"

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This type of elision is remote.

(p-550) Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and 'Asim recited "يُشْرِكُونَ" with a ya' from below, while the people of Madina, Makka and Kufa recited with a ta' from above.

His saying: ﴿Is not He who created﴾ and what follows of these interrogations is a rebuke to them, and an affirmation of what they have no escape from acknowledging. The majority recited "أمَّنَ" (amman) with a doubled mim, which is "am" entering upon "man". Al-A'mash recited "أمَن" (aman) with a fathah on the mim, eased. It is possible, on this reading, that the alif is an interrogative particle and "min" is a new beginning (mubtada'), with the predicate estimated as: "He disbelieves His blessing and associates others with Him?" and similar in meaning. "Al-hada'iq" (gardens) are gatherings of trees, of grapes, palms, and other things. Some said: one does not say "hadiqa" except for what has a wall encircling it; others said: one says it whether there is a wall or not, because the enclosure surrounds the trees. "Al-bahja" is beauty and freshness. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "ذَواتِ بَهْجَةٍ" (dhawat bahjatin). Then He, glorified be He, informed by way of interrogation that it was not for humankind, that is, it was not within their capacity nor under their power, to cause its trees to grow, because that would be bringing something from non-existence into existence. The recitation of the two hamzas in His saying "أئِنَّ" and "﴿أإنَّكَ لأنْتَ يُوسُفُ﴾" [Yusuf: 90] has already been discussed. As for His saying "أإلَهٌ" (a-ilahun), Abu Hatim said: the recitation with the two hamzas together is a later innovation, not found in the speech of the Arabs, and no ancient reciter read with it. "Ya'dilun" may mean: they deviate from the path of truth, that is, they act unjustly in their conduct; and it may mean: they equate others with Allah, that is, they make for Him an equal and a like.

"Khilaluha" means: between it and within it. "Al-rawasi" are the mountains; "rasa al-shay'" means a thing becomes firm and rooted when it is established. "Al-bahrān" are the sweet water in its entirety and the salt water in its entirety. "Al-hajiz" (p-551) is what Allah placed between them of barriers and obstacles of the earth, in some places thin and delicate, which, were it not for the power of Allah, blessed and exalted, the salt would overcome the sweet. Whatever has been said earlier concerning the interpretation of His saying, ﴿He let loose the two seas﴾ [al-Furqan: 53], applies here as well, so consider it. The rest of the verse is clear.
