Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verses 62–66:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿Or who answers the one in distress when he calls upon Him, and removes the evil, and makes you successors on the earth? Is there a god with Allah? Little do you remember.﴾ ﴿Or who guides you in the darknesses of land and sea, and who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy? Is there a god with Allah? Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿Or who originates creation and then repeats it, and who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Is there a god with Allah? Say: Bring your proof, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah, and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected.﴾ ﴿Rather, their knowledge has followed up concerning the Hereafter. Rather, they are in doubt about it. Rather, they are blind to it.﴾

In these verses He made them consider the meanings by which it becomes clear to every intelligent person that no idol and no false god has any place in them. They are lessons and blessings, so the proof is established by them from both aspects.

As for His words, ﴿answers the one in distress﴾, their meaning is: on the condition that He wills, according to the belief in answering. However, the one in distress is not answered, whenever he is answered, except by Allah, Mighty and Majestic. As for "al-su'" (the evil), it is general, covering every harm that Allah, Exalted, removes from His servants.

Al-Hasan read "wa-yaj'alukum" (and He makes you) with a ya' in the form of the imperfect (future), and it is also related from him with a nun. Every generation is a successor (khalaf) to the one before it. Most readers read "tadhakkarun" (you remember) with a ta', in address. Abu 'Amr alone, al-Hasan and al-A'mash read it with a ya', in the third person. "Al-zulumat" (the darknesses) is general: it includes the darkness of the night, which is the literal meaning in the language, and the darkness of ignorance, error and fear, which are figurative expressions and comparisons. This is like the saying of the poet:

"The blindnesses of men have cleared away from youth..."

And as you say: "The matter darkened" and "The matter became clear." The disagreement of the readers concerning His word "bushran" (as glad tidings) has already been mentioned. Al-Hasan and others read "yushrikun" (they associate) with a ya', in the third person, while most readers read "tushrikun" (you associate), in address.

"Bad' al-khalq" (the beginning of creation) is its invention and bringing into existence. "Al-khalq" here means the created thing from all things. But what is intended is the children of Adam, in view of the mention of repetition and resurrection from the graves. It is possible that by "al-khalq" he means the verbal noun of "khalaqa yakhluqu" (to create), and that "yabda'" (originates) and "yu'id" (repeats) are metaphors for perfection and excellence, as you say: "So-and-so originates and repeats in such-and-such a matter," meaning he perfects it. As for "al-rizq" (provision) from the heaven, it is by rain, and from the earth by plants. This is well known, as humans perceive it. And how much subtle, hidden kindness Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has!

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His Prophet to make them consider that the unseen is among the things Allah, Mighty and Majestic, alone possesses. For this reason it is called "ghayb" (unseen), because it is hidden from created beings. It is related that this verse, from His words ﴿Say: None knows﴾, was revealed because the disbelievers asked and insisted about the time of the Resurrection which he promised them. So this verse was revealed to submit to the command of Allah, Exalted, and to leave off specifying a time. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, informed that none knows the time of the Hour except Him. So He used a wording that includes the listener and others. He informed about the human beings that they do not perceive when they will be resurrected. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, used this verse as evidence for her saying: "Whoever claims that Muhammad knows the unseen has greatly slandered Allah." The word written in His words "illa Allah" (except Allah) is a substitute (badal) for "man" (none). Most people read "ayyana" (when) with a fatha on the hamza, while Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "iyyana" with a kasra on it. These are two dialects.

Most people read "bal idda-raka" (rather, has followed up). Its original form is "tadaraka," the ta' was assimilated into the dal after being changed, and then the hamza of connection was needed. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "tadaraka," as is related from him. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "bal iddaraka" on the pattern of "ifta'ala," which has the meaning of "tafa'ala." Sulayman ibn Yasar and 'Ata' ibn Yasar read "bal iddaraka" with a fatha on the lam, without a hamza, and with a shadda on the dal without an alif. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makka read "bal adraka" (rather, has reached). In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "am tadaraka 'ilmuhum" (or has their knowledge followed up). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read "bal adraka," and Ibn 'Abbas also read "bal a-iddaraka" with a hamza and a long vowel as an interrogative. Ibn Muhaysin read "bal a-addaraka" as an interrogative. Abu 'Amr al-Dani attributed it to Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

As for the reading in the interrogative form, it is in the sense of mocking the disbelievers and rebuking them concerning what is far removed from them, meaning: Has their knowledge reached the matter of the Hereafter? As for the first reading, it may carry two meanings. One: "Rather, their knowledge has reached," meaning it has ended, as you say: "The plant has reached (its maturity)" and as you say: "This is what my knowledge has reached of such-and-such." Thus their knowledge of the Hereafter has followed and ended, so that they would know a measure for it and believe, but they only have false assumptions, or they do not know a time for it. The same applies to "iddaraka," "tadaraka" and others. If this reading is taken to carry the sense of a rebuke and interrogation, it is acceptable, and it comes as a denial, because they have not attained anything beneficial. The second meaning: "Rather, it has reached" in the sense of "it reaches," meaning that in the Hereafter their knowledge will reach it at the time of the Resurrection, and they will see the punishment and the realities they denied. As for in this world, they will not. This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and al-Zajjaj inclined to it. So His words ﴿in the Hereafter﴾, according to this interpretation, are an adverbial phrase of time. According to the first interpretation, "fi" has the meaning of "ba'" (in the sense of "with" or "about"). Knowledge may also take a preposition, as you say: "My knowledge increases by such-and-such," and from it is the saying of the poet:

"And my knowledge of the markings of the waters..." (the rest of the line)

Then He described them, Mighty and Majestic, as being in doubt about it, and then followed this with a description stronger than doubt, which is complete blindness concerning the matter of the Hereafter. The original form of "'amun" (blind) is "'amiyun," on the pattern of "fa'ilun," like "hadhirun" and others.

The phrase "وَما مِن غائِبَةٍ" is grammatically an intensive form: the *ta'* in *ghā'ibah* is for emphasis (*li-l-mubālaghah*), meaning that there is nothing in the most hidden and concealed of unseen things except that it is in a Book with God, in the treasury of His knowledge. Then He, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that this Qur'an informed the Children of Israel of most of the matters about which they had disagreed concerning their descriptions, and so they came in the Qur'an as they really are. Then He described it as guidance and mercy for the believers, just as it blinded the disbelievers who were destined for it. The meaning of that is that their disbelief became entrenched despite the establishment of proof and the clarity of the path, so their blindness increased because of this proof. Then He informed that all of that is by a decree from God, exalted is He, and a judgement that He decreed concerning them and between them. Then He commanded him to rely upon Him, to trust in God, and that he is upon the truth, meaning: you are the one worthy of victory and triumph. Then He consoled him regarding them, and compared them to the dead in terms of benefit, since speaking to these and those is ineffective. So He compared them once to the dead and once to the deaf. The scholars said: the dead among the living is the one who meets God, exalted is He, in his disbelief.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

'Ā'ishah, may God be pleased with her, used this verse as evidence in denying that the Prophet ﷺ made the dead of Badr hear. She reasoned about the matter by rational analogy (*qiyās ʿaqlī*) and stopped at this verse. It is authentically established that the Prophet ﷺ said: "You are not more able to hear than they are." It seems that the story of Badr was a breach of the customary order for the Prophet ﷺ, in that God returned to them a perception by which they heard his speech. Had it not been for the Messenger of God ﷺ informing us that they heard, we would have taken his calling out to them as a rebuke to those of the disbelievers who remained, and as a means of relieving the hearts of the Muslims from them. This verse has been opposed by the greeting of peace upon graves, and by what has been narrated on this matter, that the spirits are at times at the edges of the graves. They said: if the dead person did not hear, he would not be greeted with peace.

Some narrated from Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān that it will emerge three times. It has been narrated that it is a hairy, downy beast. It has been narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, that it has the form of human beings, is in the clouds, and its legs are on the earth. It has been narrated that it combines the creation of every animal. al-Thaʿlabī mentioned something similar from Ibn al-Zubayr. It has also been narrated that it is a beast whose kind is scattered over the earth, so it emerges in every land and among every people. Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, and al-Jaḥdarī. Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "All of that, by God, it does: it speaks to them and wounds them."

It has been narrated in this regard that it passes among the people and marks the disbeliever on his forehead, blackens him, insults him, and perhaps crushes him, and perhaps wipes over the face of the believer and whitens it. After that, faith and disbelief are recognized by means of it.

It is also possible that this is part of the speech of God, mighty and majestic is He.

The meaning of that is that their disbelief became entrenched despite the establishment of proof and the clarity of the path, so their blindness increased because of this proof. Then He commanded him to rely upon Him, to trust in God, and that he is upon the truth, meaning: you are the one worthy of victory and triumph. The scholars said: the dead among the living is the one who meets God, exalted is He, in his disbelief.

They said: if the dead person did not hear, he would not be greeted with peace.

This is like his saying, upon him be blessings and peace, about the dead when he entered their place: "They hear the sound of sandals."

The majority of readers read: "*inna al-nāsa*" with a *kasrah* on *inna*. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, and ʿĀṣim read with a *fatḥah* on the *alif*. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: "*tukallimuhum bi-anna*," and this is an affirmation (*taṣdīq*) with the *fatḥah*. According to this reading, His saying: ﴿that the people﴾ up to the end of the verse is part of the speech of the beast. This has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both. It is also possible that this is part of the speech of God, mighty and majestic is He.

The phrase "وَما مِن غائِبَةٍ" is grammatically an intensive form: the *ta'* in *ghā'ibah* is for emphasis (*li-l-mubālaghah*), meaning that there is nothing in the most hidden and concealed of unseen things except that it is in a Book with God, in the treasury of His knowledge. Then He, exalted is He, drew attention to the fact that this Qur'an informed the Children of Israel of most of the matters about which they had disagreed concerning their descriptions, and so they came in the Qur'an as they really are. Then He described it as guidance and mercy for the believers, just as it blinded the disbelievers who were destined for it. The meaning of that is that their disbelief became entrenched despite the establishment of proof and the clarity of the path, so their blindness increased because of this proof. Then He informed that all of that is by a decree from God, exalted is He, and a judgement that He decreed concerning them and between them. Then He commanded him to rely upon Him, to trust in God, and that he is upon the truth, meaning: you are the one worthy of victory and triumph. Then He consoled him regarding them, and compared them to the dead in terms of benefit, since speaking to these and those is ineffective. So He compared them once to the dead and once to the deaf. The scholars said: the dead among the living is the one who meets God, exalted is He, in his disbelief.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

'Ā'ishah, may God be pleased with her, used this verse as evidence in denying that the Prophet ﷺ made the dead of Badr hear. She reasoned about the matter by rational analogy (*qiyās ʿaqlī*) and stopped at this verse. It is authentically established that the Prophet ﷺ said: "You are not more able to hear than they are." It seems that the story of Badr was a breach of the customary order for the Prophet ﷺ, in that God returned to them a perception by which they heard his speech. Had it not been for the Messenger of God ﷺ informing us that they heard, we would have taken his calling out to them as a rebuke to those of the disbelievers who remained, and as a means of relieving the hearts of the Muslims from them. This verse has been opposed by the greeting of peace upon graves, and by what has been narrated on this matter, that the spirits are at times at the edges of the graves. They said: if the dead person did not hear, he would not be greeted with peace.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

All of this does not contradict the verse, because greeting peace upon graves is an act of worship, and God has the reward for it. It is a reminder to oneself of the state of death and of the state of the dead in their lives. Even if we permit, alongside this, that spirits are at times upon the graves, then if the dead person hears, it is not that the spirit is dead. Rather, what is meant by His saying: ﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾ is the bodily persons separated from their spirits. And concerning this we say: the customary order was breached for Muhammad ﷺ regarding the people of the well (*al-qalīb*). This is like his saying, upon him be blessings and peace, about the dead when he entered their place: "They hear the sound of sandals."

Ibn Kathīr read: "*wa-lā yusmiʿu*" with a *yā'* from below, *al-ṣumm* in the nominative, and similarly in al-Rūm. The rest read: "*tusmiʿu*" with a *tā'*, *al-ṣumm* in the accusative. The majority of readers read: "*wa-mā anta bi-hādī al-ʿumy*" with the genitive construction (*idāfah*). Yaḥyā ibn al-Ḥārith and Abū Ḥaywah read: "*bi-hādin al-ʿumy*" with tanwīn on the *dāl* and *al-ʿumya* in the accusative. Ḥamzah alone read: "*wa-mā anta tahdī al-ʿumy*" with an imperfect verb; this is the reading of Ṭalḥah ibn Wathhāb and Ibn Yaʿmur. In the codex (*muṣḥaf*) of ʿAbd Allāh: "*wa-mā an tahdiya al-ʿumy*."

The meaning of His saying: ﴿And when the word comes to pass against them﴾ is: when the promise of their punishment, which the word contained now from God in that regard, is fulfilled, meaning when He has made it binding upon them and decreed it. This is equivalent to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The word of punishment has come to pass﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. So the meaning of the verse is: when God, exalted is He, wills to carry out upon the disbelievers the punishment of His foreknowledge concerning them, He will bring forth for them a beast from the earth. It has been narrated that this will be when good is cut off, when no one is commanded to do what is right nor forbidden from what is wrong, and no one who repents or turns back remains, just as God revealed to Noah: ﴿that none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [Hūd: 36]. The verb "*waqaʿa*" is an expression for establishment and necessity. In a ḥadīth: "Indeed, the beast and the rising of the sun from the west are the first of the signs," and he did not specify which comes first; and likewise the Dajjāl.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of the ḥadīths and narrations is that the sun is the last of them, because repentance ends with it. The situation indicates that faith remains only in individuals, and upon them blows the wind that leaves no faith, and at that point it is exhausted, and the Trumpet is blown. We narrate that the beast will mark a people with faith, and we find that ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, upon him be peace, descends after the Dajjāl, and people believe in him. It has been narrated that this beast will emerge from Mount al-Ṣafā in Mecca. This was said by ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, may God be pleased with them both, said something similar, and said: "If I wished to place my foot upon the place of its emergence, I would do so." It has been narrated from Qatādah that it will emerge in Tihāmah. It has been narrated that it will emerge from the mosque of Kufa, from the place where the oven of Noah boiled over. Some narrated from Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān that it will emerge three times. It has been narrated that it is a hairy, downy beast. It has been narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, that it has the form of human beings, is in the clouds, and its legs are on the earth. It has been narrated that it combines the creation of every animal. al-Thaʿlabī mentioned something similar from Ibn al-Zubayr. It has also been narrated that it is a beast whose kind is scattered over the earth, so it emerges in every land and among every people. So His saying, according to this interpretation, "*dābbah*" (a beast) is a generic noun. Al-Naqqāsh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, that it is the serpent that overlooked the wall of the Kaʿbah, which the eagles snatched away when Quraysh wanted to rebuild the Kaʿbah.

The majority of people read: "*tukallimuhum*" from speech (*al-kalām*). In the codex of Ubayy: "*tunbiʾuhum*." ʿIkrimah interpreted it as "*tasimuhum*" (she marks them). Qatādah said: in some readings it is "*tuḥaddithuhum*." Abū Zarʿah ibn ʿAmr ibn Jurayj read: "*tukalmihim*" with a *kasrah* on the *lām*, from *al-kalm*, which is a wound. Abū al-Fatḥ said: this is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, and al-Jaḥdarī. Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, said: "All of that, by God, it does: it speaks to them and wounds them."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 27, verse 83–87:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And on the Day when We shall gather from every nation a troop of those who denied Our signs, and they will be driven in ranks,﴾ ﴿until, when they have come, He will say, "Did you deny My signs while you did not encompass them in knowledge? Or what was it that you were doing?"﴾ ﴿And the word will fall upon them because of what they wronged, and they will not speak.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen that We made the night for them to rest therein and the day giving sight? Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe.﴾ ﴿And the Day the Horn is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills. And all will come to Him humbled.﴾

The meaning: "Remember the Day" — this is a reminder of the Day of Resurrection. "Nahshuru" means we gather. "From every nation" intends: from every generation of earlier people, since no era has been free of disbelievers in Allah from the time the children of Adam dispersed. "Al-fawj" is a large group of people, and the meaning is: those whose state is that they deny Our signs. "Yuza'un" means they are restrained in the driving, that is, their first is held back until their last, as said by Qatadah and others, and from it comes "waazi' al-jaysh" (the one who restrains the army). In this the poet 'Abd al-Sharif ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza says:

؎ They came upon us like a cold cloud, and at times like a flood, riding in front of those who restrain them.

Then Most High informs about His halting the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection and questioning them in the manner of rebuke: "Until, when..." the verse, then He said, "Or what was it that you were doing?" in the sense of exhausting the proofs, that is: if you have any deed or proof, then bring it forth. Abu Haywa read: "Amadha kuntum ta'maluna" with the mim lightened.

Then He informs about the word falling upon them, that is, the execution of the punishment and the decree being final, and that they will not speak with a proof, because it is not theirs. This is in one of the stations of the Resurrection and concerns a group of people, because the Qur'an implies that they speak with proofs in other than this station.

Then He mentioned the sign in the night and its being a time of stillness and tranquility for all living creatures, and the important part in that is the children of Adam; and the day being "giving sight," that is, possessing sight. This is like when you say: "a night standing and a day fasting," and the meaning of that is: it is stood in during it; similarly this means: it is seen in during it, so it is, for that reason, possessing sight. Then it is used figuratively to say "mubsiran" (giving sight), so it is on the pattern of an attributive noun, like "'ishatin radiyatin" (a pleasing life). The signs in that are for both believers and disbelievers; it is a sign for all of them in itself, but in terms of benefiting from it and reflecting profitably, it is only for the believers, so they alone are singled out for mention.

Then Blessed and Most High mentioned the Day of the blowing into the Horn (al-Sur), which is the horn according to the saying of the majority of the community, and which is what the narrations imply. Mujahid said: it is like the shape of a trumpet. A group said: "al-Sur" is the plural of "surah," like "tamrah" and "tamr" and "jamrah" and "jamr." The first is more famous. In the widely transmitted narrations, Israfil, peace be upon him, is the holder of the Horn; he has crouched on one knee, raised the other, inclined his cheek, and put the horn to his mouth, awaiting when he will be commanded and given permission to blow. The blast mentioned in this verse is the blast of terror. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the angel has three blasts: the blast of terror, which is the terror of worldly life and not the greatest terror; the blast of swooning; and the blast of rising from the graves. Another group said: there are only two blasts, as though they made the terror and the swooning into one blast, and they cited the saying of the Most High: ﴿Then it will be blown again, and immediately they will be standing, looking on﴾ [al-Zumar: 68], and they said: "ukhra" is not said except of the second.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The first opinion is more correct; "ukhra" is also said of the third, and from it is the saying of Rabi'ah ibn Maqrum:

"And indeed I doubled them with a third last one"

And from it is the saying of the Most High: ﴿and Manat, the third, the other﴾ [al-Najm: 20]. As for the saying of the poet:

؎ I made for her two sticks of nasham and another of thumamah

it may be that he means a second or a third, so there is no proof in it.

The saying of the Most High: ﴿fa-fazi'a﴾ (so terror will seize) — and it is a matter that has not yet occurred — is taken as an indication of the certainty of its occurrence, and this is the meaning of placing the past tense in the position of the future. The saying of the Most High: ﴿except whom Allah wills﴾ is an exception concerning those whom Allah has decreed among His angels, prophets and the martyrs among His servants, that the terror of the blast of the Horn will not reach them. Abu Hurayrah said: it refers to the martyrs. Al-Rummani mentioned that it is the Prophet ﷺ. Muqatil said: it refers to Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and the Angel of Death. And if the greatest terror does not reach them, they are more deserving that this will not reach them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Yet this is at a time of anticipation, and that is at a time of security, since it is the closing of Hell upon its people.

The majority of reciters read: "wa kullun atawhu dakhirin" on the pattern of "fa'iluhu," while Hamzah and Hafs from 'Asim read: "atawhu" in the form of the past verb, and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and the people of Kufa. Qatadah read: "atahu" in the singular, following the wording "kull," and Al-Zajjaj alluded to this reading without mentioning it.

"Al-dakhir" is one who is humbled and submissive. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said: "al-dakhir" is the abased. Al-Hasan read: "dakhirin" without an alif. The reports are consistent that the exception in this verse is meant to refer to the martyrs, because they are alive with their Lord, being provided for, and they are of the kind that feels terror, since they are human, but they were given preference by security on that Day.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And you see the mountains, you think them solid, while they pass away as the passing of clouds. [It is] the handiwork of Allah, who has perfected everything. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it, and they will be safe from the terror of that Day.﴾ ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire. Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, which He has made sacred, and to Him belongs everything. And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims,﴾ ﴿and to recite the Qur'an. So whoever is guided, it is only for his own soul that he is guided; and whoever goes astray, say, "I am only one of the warners."﴾ ﴿And say, "Praise be to Allah. He will show you His signs, and you will recognize them. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do."﴾

This describes the condition of things on the Day of Resurrection after the blowing of the Trumpet. The seeing is with the eye. This is the state of the mountains at the beginning of the matter: they move and sway, and by the command of Allah, blessed and exalted, they are blown away and scattered during that time, so they become like wool, and then at the very end they become scattered dust (haba' munbath). "Al-Jumud" (solidity) is the firmness of substance. Ibn 'Abbas said: "jamidah" means "standing." Its parallel is the saying of the poet:

؎ With a massive one like a mountain, you think they are standing still for a pilgrim, while the riders are pacing smoothly.

(p-565) "Sun'a Allah" (the handiwork of Allah) is a definite verbal noun (masdar), and its governing verb is an implied verb of the same root. It was said that it is in the accusative as an incitement (al-ighra'), meaning: "Look at the handiwork of Allah." "Al-Itqan" (perfection) is doing well in what is made, and that it be good and of firm strength. Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "yaf'alun" with the ya' (third person), while the rest read "taf'alun" with the ta' (second person address).

"Al-Hasanah" (the good deed) is faith. Al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i and Qatadah said: it is "There is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah). It is narrated from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn that he said: "I was in some of my solitary moments, and I raised my voice with 'La ilaha illa Allah,' and I heard someone saying: 'It is the word about which Allah said: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed will have better than it.﴾'" His saying ﴿better than it﴾ may be understood as a comparative, and in His saying "minha" (than it) there is an omitted noun, its estimate being: "better than its measure or its deserved reward," meaning that Allah bestows on him beyond what his good deed deserves. Ibn Zayd said: "He is given ten for one." The motive for this estimate is that no comparison can be conceived between the good deed and the reward. It may also be that "khayr" is not comparative, but a name for reward and blessing, and His saying "minha" is for the starting point of the end (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning: this recompense which he receives is from his good deed and because of it. This is the saying of al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj. 'Ikrimah said: "Nothing is better than 'There is no god but Allah,' but for him is the good from it."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "min faza'in yawma'idhin" with the genitive construction (idafah). They then differed over the vowel of the mim in "yawma'idhin": most of them read it with a fatha on the mim, as the adverb is built (mabni) because it is attached to a non-declinable (ghayr mumkin) word, and Isma'il ibn Ja'far, from Nafi', read it with a kasra on the mim, applying the genitive construction. That is because adverbs, when attached to a non-declinable word, may be built and the genitive force applied to them. Of this is the poet's saying:

؎ At the time when I reproached grey hair over youth, and I said: "Will I not wake up while the white hair restrains me?"

(p-566) It is narrated as "'ala hina" with a fatha on the nun, and "'ala hinin" with a kasra. Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "min fazi'in" with tanwin and without the genitive construction, and with this reading it is only permissible to read the mim of "yawma'idhin" with a fatha.

"Al-Sayyi'ah" (the evil deed) in this verse is disbelief and sins of those whom Allah, exalted, has decreed to enter the Fire from among the people of His will. "Kabb" means: they were thrown into the Fire, and this came as "kabban," from the standpoint of its creation in this world, which gives the sense of raising. When the faces are thrown down, the rest of the body is more fit to enter the Fire, since the face is the place of honour and the senses. His saying ﴿Are you recompensed?﴾ means: He said that to them, and this is in the manner of rebuke.

His saying ﴿Indeed, I have been commanded﴾ means: Say, O Muhammad, to your people: "Indeed, I have been commanded." The city referred to is Makkah. The majority of people read "alladhi harramaha" (which He made sacred). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read "allati harramaha" (which is made sacred), and in this verse He attributed the sanctification to Allah, exalted, insofar as it is by His decree and prior knowledge. The Prophet ﷺ attributed it to Ibrahim in his saying: "Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I have made Madinah sacred," insofar as its apparent meaning was by his supplication, his desire and his conveying it to his community. So there is no contradiction between the verse and the hadith. In His saying "harramaha" there is an enumeration of His blessing upon Quraysh, in that Allah, exalted, lifted from their land the raids and the widespread strife across all the lands of the Arabs.

His, exalted, saying ﴿and to Him belongs everything﴾ means: by dominion and servitude. The majority of people read "an aku" (that I should recite) as conjoined to His saying "an akuna" (that I should be). Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-an-ta'lu al-Qur'an" meaning: and it was said to me: "Recite the Qur'an." "Ti'la" means: follow with your recitation among its verses and string them together. The recitation of the Qur'an is the cause of being guided to every good.

His, exalted, saying ﴿So whoever is guided﴾ means: whoever earns guidance and faith and considers in a way that saves him, then his effort is for his own self.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The attribution of guidance and misguidance to humans in this verse is only by acquisition (kasb), by greed, and by the state upon which reward and punishment occur. And all of it is also from Allah, exalted, by origination (al-ikhtira').

The recitation of the Qur'an is the cause of being guided to every good.

His, exalted, saying ﴿So whoever is guided﴾ means: whoever earns guidance and faith and considers in a way that saves him, then his effort is for his own self.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The attribution of guidance and misguidance to humans in this verse is only by acquisition (kasb), by greed, and by the state upon which reward and punishment occur. And all of it is also from Allah, exalted, by origination (al-ikhtira').

His, exalted, saying ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ is a threat of the punishment of this world, such as Badr and the Conquest and the like, and of the punishment of the Hereafter. The majority of reciters read "'amma ya'maluna" with the ya', while Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim read "'amma ta'maluna" with the ta' from above, addressing them directly.

The Tafsir of Surah an-Naml is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
